conversation:
Patient: Hi, I'm Beverly. I'm not sure about my exact age, but I'm in my late 30s or early 40s. I came in because I fell off my tandem bike about two weeks ago, and my right knee has been hurting ever since. It's been sore and aching daily, and I'm worried something might be wrong with it.
Doctor: Could you confirm your exact age and gender, and describe the nature of the pain in your right knee? Have you noticed any swelling, stiffness, or difficulty bearing weight on it?
Patient: I'm female, and I'm 38 years old. The pain is a constant ache, especially when I walk or go up hills. It doesn't really swell, but it feels unstable sometimes, like it might shift when I'm walking. It's hard to put weight on it without it hurting.
Doctor: Have you undergone any imaging or medical evaluations for your knee injury since the fall?
Patient: Yes, I had x-rays done today, and the doctor looked at them. He said the x-rays looked pretty normal, but he still thinks I might have injured my posterior cruciate ligament. He wants me to get an MRI to check for any other issues like a meniscus tear or cartilage damage.
Doctor: Have you experienced any locking, catching, or giving way of the knee since the injury?
Patient: No, I haven't experienced any locking or catching, but sometimes it feels like it shifts when I walk, which is pretty unsettling. It doesn't really give way completely, but it's not stable either.
Doctor: Could you describe the specific location of the pain in your right knee and whether it radiates to other areas?
Patient: The pain is on the inside of my right knee, right along the medial joint line. It doesn't really radiate anywhere else, just stays right there. It's pretty tender when touched, and it hurts more when I walk up hills or put weight on it.
Doctor: Could you describe any specific movements or activities that make the pain worse or better? Have you noticed any locking, clicking, or popping sensations in the knee?
Patient: The pain gets worse when I walk up hills or put weight on it, and it's especially tender on the inside of my knee. I haven't noticed any locking or popping, but sometimes it feels like it shifts when I'm walking, which is pretty unsettling.
Doctor: Have you undergone any ligament testing, such as Lachman's test, anterior drawer test, or posterior drawer test, to assess the stability of your knee?
Patient: The doctor did do some testing on my knee. He checked the ligaments and said the medial collateral ligament is intact, and there's a little laxity in the posterior drawer. He compared it to my other knee and said it feels a bit unstable, but nothing too severe. He didn't do the Lachman test specifically, but he did mention that the anterior drawer was negative.
Doctor: Thank you for sharing that information. To better understand your condition, could you tell me if you've noticed any locking or catching sensations in your knee, or if there are specific activities that make the pain worse?
Patient: I haven't noticed any locking or catching sensations in my knee, but the pain definitely gets worse when I walk up hills or put weight on it. It's especially tender on the inside of my knee, and sometimes it feels like it shifts when I'm walking, which is pretty unsettling.
Doctor: Has the patient undergone any previous imaging studies for the knee, such as an MRI or ultrasound, prior to this incident?
Patient: No, I haven't had any imaging studies done for my knee before this incident. The doctor did take some x-rays today, and they looked pretty normal, but he thinks I might need an MRI to get a better look at what's going on inside the knee.
Doctor: Thank you for confirming that you haven't had any prior imaging for your knee. Since the X-rays were normal, the next step is to proceed with an MRI to evaluate for possible meniscus tear or cartilage damage. Is there anything else you'd like to share about your symptoms or concerns before we move forward with the MRI?
Patient: No, I don't think there's anything else to share right now. The main thing is that I want to get better and get back to walking my dog and doing my job without pain. I just hope it doesn't require surgery.
Doctor: Thank you for sharing your concerns, Beverly. I understand how important it is for you to get back to your daily activities without pain. Since the MRI is pending, I would like to ask if there are any other symptoms or concerns you have not yet mentioned that might be relevant to your knee condition?
Patient: No, I don't think there's anything else to share right now. The main thing is that I want to get better and get back to walking my dog and doing my job without pain. I just hope it doesn't require surgery.
Doctor: Thank you for sharing your concerns. I understand how important it is for you to get back to your daily activities without pain. To better understand your condition and ensure we get the most accurate MRI results, could you describe the exact location of the tenderness on the medial joint line of your right knee and whether there is any associated warmth or redness?
Patient: The tenderness is right on the inside of my knee, along the medial joint line. It's pretty sore when he touches it, but I don't think there's any warmth or redness there. It just feels really tender and a little swollen.
Doctor: Thank you for the details. Could you please describe the exact nature of the shifting sensation you feel in your knee when walking? For example, does it feel like the knee is buckling, giving way, or shifting to one side? Also, have you noticed any changes in your range of motion or difficulty fully straightening or bending your knee?
Patient: The shifting sensation feels like the knee is kind of sliding or moving a little to the side when I walk, and it's not super obvious, but it's enough to make me feel unstable. I can still straighten and bend it all the way, but sometimes it clicks when I do, and it feels a little weak when I'm going up hills.
Doctor: Could you please describe how often you experience the shifting sensation in your knee and whether it occurs during specific activities? Also, have you noticed any locking or catching in your knee, even if it's not frequent?
Patient: The shifting sensation happens pretty often when I'm walking, especially on uneven ground or when I'm turning. It doesn't happen all the time, but it's enough to make me feel like the knee isn't stable. I haven't noticed any locking or catching, just that odd sliding feeling and the clicking sometimes.
Doctor: Could you describe the nature of the clicking sensation in your knee when you bend or straighten it? Is it a sharp click, a soft snap, or something else? Also, have you noticed any changes in your range of motion, such as difficulty fully bending or straightening your knee?
Patient: The clicking is more like a soft snap when I bend or straighten it, not really sharp. And I can still bend and straighten it all the way, but sometimes it feels a little stiff, especially in the morning.
